claims.text: As-built laser-additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components can contain residual porosity.
As-built additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components can contain fabrication-induced microcracks.
Rapid solidification and thermal gradients cause dimensional distortion in additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components.
HIP at approximately 1100–1200 °C and 100–200 MPa, followed by controlled cooling, will reduce porosity and heal microcracks in additively manufactured high-entropy alloys.
A controlled inert atmosphere during HIP will avoid oxidation.
HIP can uniformly act throughout additively manufactured parts having typical geometries and defect levels.
Elevated temperature during HIP enhances diffusion that heals microvoids and cracks.
HIP produces a more uniform, refined, and densified microstructure with fewer internal defects.
The combination of high temperature and isostatic pressure accelerates mass transport.
HIP reduces residual stresses in additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components.
Eliminating internal stress concentrators and homogenizing the microstructure improves mechanical integrity.
HIP-induced densification reduces dimensional deviations.
HIP-treated components will have higher overall density than as-built controls.
HIP-treated components will have less shrinkage or distortion and better dimensional accuracy than as-built controls.
HIP-treated components will have greater tensile or compressive strength than as-built controls.
HIP-treated components will have greater hardness than as-built controls.
Porosity and microcracks in as-built components cause dimensional inaccuracies and reduced mechanical performance.
Extremely high initial porosity or geometries that inhibit uniform HIP action may limit treatment efficacy.
Optimal HIP parameters vary with alloy composition and component geometry.
The predicted treatment effect includes at least a 10% reduction in porosity and at least a 15% increase in mechanical strength.
